# My Playbook for ref_estate

**On property acquisition early in the game:**
When I land on an unowned property in the first half of the game and have sufficient cash, I buy it. Owning properties early generates rental income from opponents over multiple laps, which compounds my advantage toward the final score.

**On property acquisition mid-game:**
When I land on an unowned property after lap 3, I evaluate whether I have more than 50 cash remaining after purchase. If yes, I buy. If no, I pass. The end-game is too close to overextend on cash.

**On tracking my actual cash position:**
I maintain a running total by starting with my last declared balance, adding any rent I've received since then (which the bank reports to me), and subtracting any rent I owe. I declare this sum honestly before deciding whether I can afford to buy.

**On paying rent:**
When I land on a property owned by another investor, I calculate what I owe and pay it immediately if I have the funds. I do not avoid or postpone this payment.

**On the final lap:**
On lap 6, I collect my salary if I pass START and do not buy properties. My score is determined by my declared cash plus the purchase prices of the deeds I hold, so preserving cash is irrelevant—only the deeds matter. I should have bought more properties earlier when I had the chance.

**On opportunity cost:**
I failed to acquire enough properties in my playthrough. I had cash available in lap 5 but declined to buy, which was a mistake. When I land on an unowned property and have over 50 cash remaining, I should buy it, even late in the game. Properties on the deed sheet count toward my final score regardless of when I purchase them.

# Playbook for ref_estate

**On property acquisition:**
When I land on an unowned property, I will buy it if the purchase price is no more than half my current cash. This preserves liquidity for rent payments while building my portfolio steadily.

**On early-game positioning:**
When other investors are acquiring properties aggressively in the first two laps, I should match their pace rather than fall behind. Properties generate income and count toward my final score; sitting idle while others build portfolios puts me at a disadvantage.

**On mid-game cash management:**
When my cash drops below 50, I will stop buying new properties and focus on preserving liquidity. Rent payments to well-developed opponents become more likely, and I need reserves to handle them without being forced into negative positions.

**On late-game property decisions:**
When I'm in the final two laps and my cash is marginal (below 75), I will decline to buy even moderately-priced properties. The endgame scoring is based on declared cash plus deed values; being caught with insufficient cash to pay rent is worse than missing a late purchase.

**On salary collection:**
When I pass START, I will add that salary to my declared balance immediately and track it carefully. This is reliable income that should factor into my purchasing decisions on the same turn.

**On tracking and honesty:**
I will maintain accurate accounting of my cash at every turn, including all transfers received. The scoring system depends on my declared balance, so precision here is essential to avoiding self-inflicted losses.

**What did not work:**
Passing on the Quarry purchase in lap 5 was reasonable caution, but I should have been more aggressive earlier when cash flow was healthier. My final score of 201 suggests I ended with strong cash but could have accumulated more deed value by accepting slightly lower liquidity margins in laps 2-4.

# My Playbook for ref_estate

When I land on an unowned property in the early laps (laps 1-3), I buy it if I have sufficient cash. Properties generate revenue through rent, and acquiring them early gives me a larger portfolio by the end.

When I land on an owned property and owe rent, I pay the full amount owed even if it strains my cash position. The bank will record it and I declare my true balance honestly.

When I'm deciding whether to buy a property, I calculate: purchase price plus remaining laps times likely rent income I'll collect, versus the cash I need to stay solvent. If cash is very low (under 20), I skip purchases to maintain a safety buffer.

When I own properties, I expect to collect rent as other players land on them. I track this incoming revenue mentally when deciding whether to make purchases.

When I pass START, I collect my salary and add it to my declared balance immediately.

When I have negative cash, I don't panic—the game is scored on total value (cash plus property worth) at the end, and I can recover if I own enough properties that generate rent in the remaining laps.

I should have been more conservative about spending down to nearly zero cash in the middle laps. The purchase of Mill for 90 when I had only 92 left me dangerously exposed and unable to pay rent when due. Next time, when my cash drops below 30, I stop buying new properties and focus on surviving the remaining laps without debt.

I should not declare negative balances if I can avoid them. If I cannot afford rent, I need to have managed my purchases differently earlier.

My final score was 207, which came from a small cash balance plus the value of the two properties I owned (Foundry and Mill). I should aim to own 3-4 properties by mid-game to maximize final score, but only if I can do so without going deeply negative on cash.
